newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan oil spill spreads but nuclear plants fine.
newsitem.headline: Japan oil spill spreads but nuclear plants fine.

text.p: A network of oil fences and favourable currents have prevented the country's worst oil spill from reaching a string of nuclear plants along Japan's northern coast, officials said on Sunday.
However, a new slick estimated at 20 km (12 miles) long was spotted east of the main concentration of oil, possibly headed for previously untouched areas.
Officials are focusing their cleanup efforts on the waters near 15 nuclear power plants, the world's largest concentration of nuclear power generation.

The sea water is vital to keeping the reactors from over-heating. While their intake pipes are set about five metres (16 feet) below the water level, the heavy oil has been gradually sinking as it becomes as thick as mud.
While some of the oil slicks around the plants in Wakasa Bay are within a kilometre (0.6 miles) of land, none has yet to hit shore there.
"According to the first surveys Sunday morning, there are no places where the oil has hit Wakasa Bay," a spokesman for the Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) said at a morning news briefing.
"The MSA is regularly providing oil flow information to the nuclear power plants, which have all put oil fences in place," the spokesman said.

Nuclear power plant officials say there is no danger of a meltdown even if oil gets into the intake pipes. They said that the system can tolerate small amounts of oil and at worst they would have to suspend power generation.
Officials still have no firm figure on how much oil has escaped from the 13,157-tonne Russian tanker Nakhodka when it broke up in stormy seas on January 2.
They admit that the earlier estimate of 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) was too low. The 26-year-old tanker was carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of fuel oil.
The agency had 10 boats working on the cleanup in the Wakasa Bay area where more than 100 slicks have been spotted.
But new problems may be emerging elsewhere. The stern of the tanker, submerged in 2,000 metres of water and holding the bulk of the oil, may now be leaking, officials said.
A Russian oil-cleaning ship, the first of two, was dispatched from the Pacific port city of Sakhalin to help scoop up the oil. The ship is specially designed to filter oil from seawater.
Hundreds of volunteers have flocked to the areas already hit, which include some of the most fertile fishing grounds in Japan, to help in gathering the oil from shorelines.

With little more than buckets and scoops, they braved snow, sleet and cold. But medical experts said caution should be taken following reports of nausea, rashes and other ailments among some volunteers.
They said that the oil contained some toxic elements and many of the helpers on the beaches had no more than rubber gloves to protect them.
